Collectibles · Nov 25, 2026 · 7:08 AM ET

Target Pokémon drops: what they resell for

By Matt

Target puts four Pokémon 30th Celebration products in stores Saturday, November 28 — and the $31.99 Booster Bundle is the one to queue for: it resells for about $59 on eBay, roughly $19 clear after fees.

Disclosure: this post contains affiliate links. I earn a commission on qualifying purchases.

Target's Black Friday Pokémon drop lands in stores on Saturday, November 28 — the day after Black Friday — and there are four 30th Celebration products on the shelf. One of them is worth lining up for. The Booster Bundle costs $31.99 at Target and resells for about $59 on eBay, which works out to roughly $19 clear after eBay's fees. The other three are a thinner play, and one of them loses money outright.

The drop is part of Target's Black Friday sale event, which runs November 22–29. Target's own announcement confirms a Pokémon trading card game drop on November 28, with no start time given — and these are in-store items, not a midnight online restock.

The four products, ranked by resale

CardWire tracked median prices from eBay sold listings between November 14 and 24, then subtracted eBay's 13.25% selling fee plus $0.40 per order. Here's how the four Saturday items stack up:

30th Celebration Booster Bundle (6 packs): $31.99; $59; ~$19 profit

30th Celebration Figure Collection (Mew or Mewtwo): $39.99; $61; ~$13 profit

30th Celebration Tin (Sylveon ex or Greninja ex): $29.99; $43; ~$7 profit

30th Celebration Battle Deck (Espeon ex or Umbreon ex): $24.99; $25; ~$4 loss

The Booster Bundle is the clear pick: six packs for $31.99, and the only item in the drop with a comfortable margin. The Figure Collection is the runner-up — Mew and Mewtwo versions both go for $39.99, with about $13 left after fees. The tin clears a modest $7. The Battle Deck is the one to skip: it sells on eBay for essentially what Target charges, so fees eat the whole thing.

The deal is the resale, not the shelf price

None of these are discounted. Target is charging its standard prices — in some cases more than other retailers. The Booster Bundle lists at $31.99, which is $5.05 above its reported $26.94 MSRP. The Figure Collection is $39.99 at Target against $29.99 at Best Buy, and the Battle Deck is $24.99 against $19.99 there. LV1 Gaming's price comparison put it bluntly: the savings on this drop are $0.

That is the whole story of the 30th Celebration set this year. Demand is doing the work, not discounts. A November 10 TCGplayer snapshot had the Booster Bundle at $67.08 and the Mew and Mewtwo Figure Collections at $72.69 and $78.55 — higher than CardWire's eBay medians from two weeks later, but the same direction: every one of these boxes trades above what Target charges for it.

The same pattern showed up across the wider market this week. NerdSnack's Black Friday guide, updated November 24, has the standard 30th Celebration Elite Trainer Box at $113.99 against a $49.99 MSRP — more than double list — while Magic booster boxes sell for about half of theirs. Pokémon is the premium side of the hobby right now, and Target's Saturday shelf is one of the few places to buy in at retail.

If you miss Saturday

A leaked notice tracked by TCGTracker points to a second date: December 4. Nothing is confirmed beyond that, and the December 4 tin is a different item — a $21.99 tin, not the $29.99 Sylveon ex or Greninja ex version in Saturday's drop — so don't count on a straight rerun. Saturday is the shot.

NBA · Nov 25, 2026 · 3:09 AM ET

Celtics build 34-point lead, then hold off Wizards

By Matt

Jayson Tatum scored a season-high 41 points as the Celtics beat the Wizards 131-116 in Washington, snapping a four-game losing streak — after nearly giving away a 34-point lead.

Disclosure: this post contains affiliate links. I earn a commission on qualifying purchases.

Jayson Tatum scored a season-high 41 points and the Boston Celtics beat the Washington Wizards 131-116 on Tuesday night at Capital One Arena, snapping a four-game losing streak in an NBA Cup game they nearly gave away.

Boston built a 34-point lead, watched Washington cut it to five late in the fourth quarter, and steadied itself in time to close out the win. The victory moved the Celtics to 3-0 in East Group C play.

How the night unfolded

The Celtics came out firing. Tatum scored 28 of his points before halftime, shooting 9 of 13 from the field and 6 of 9 from three in the opening two quarters, and Boston won the second quarter 46-21 to take a 31-point lead into the break. Paul George added 13 in the second quarter before Tatum checked back in to score 13 of his own, and the lead peaked at 34.

Then the game flipped. Washington outscored Boston 40-24 in the third quarter, and the Wizards kept coming in the fourth, getting as close as 117-112 with 3:19 left. The Celtics held on from there, closing the final stretch to win by 15.

The win ended a four-game skid for Boston, which had gone 0-3 on its road trip coming into the night.

Jayson Tatum: 41; 6; 8; 13-25 FG, 6-15 3PT, 9-14 FT

Paul George: 28; —; 9; 11-20 FG, 6-9 3PT

Neemias Queta: 21; —; —; —

Tatum's line came with two blocks. George and Tatum combined for 69 points — more than half of Boston's total — and Queta chipped in 21 as the third scorer.

The Cup stakes

The result all but locked up Boston's place in the NBA Cup quarter-finals. At 3-0 in Group C, the Celtics sit unbeaten with one group game left — against the Atlanta Hawks on Friday, November 27. Washington, meanwhile, is mathematically eliminated from Cup play.

It also carried a milestone on the sideline: head coach Joe Mazzulla became the second-fastest head coach in NBA history to reach 250 career wins, tying Phil Jackson at 346 games.

Packers-Rams open Thanksgiving week tonight on Netflix

By Matt

The NFL plays its first-ever Thanksgiving Eve game tonight — the 6-4 Packers visit the 6-4 Rams at SoFi Stadium at 8 p.m. ET on Netflix, with U2 headlining halftime and a full five-game holiday slate to follow.

Disclosure: this post contains affiliate links. I earn a commission on qualifying purchases.

Thanksgiving football starts a day early this year. The NFL plays its first-ever Thanksgiving Eve game tonight, with Green Bay visiting Los Angeles at 8 p.m. ET on Netflix — and the matchup is a genuine playoff-shaper, not a holiday novelty act.

The matchup

Both teams come in at 6-4, tied in the thick of the NFC race, and the head-to-head history leans hard one way: Matt LaFleur is 5-0 against Sean McVay, his former boss, and Green Bay has won 10 of the last 11 meetings between the clubs, including each of the last five. The most recent one was at this same stadium — a 24-19 Packers win on Oct. 6, 2024.

Record: 6-4; 6-4

Kickoff: Tonight, 8 p.m. ET

Venue: SoFi Stadium, Inglewood, CA

TV: Netflix

Line: Rams -2.5

The form lines point in opposite directions. Los Angeles has won four straight, most recently a 34-6 rout of Arizona. Green Bay is coming off its bye after a 30-10 home loss to Minnesota — and the bye week brought a major reinforcement: Micah Parsons has been cleared and is set to make his season debut tonight.

The Rams, meanwhile, are doing it short-handed at receiver, with Puka Nacua out for the rest of the regular season. That puts even more on Matthew Stafford and the ground game in a matchup where the Packers' pass rush just got its best player back.

A new holiday tradition

This is the start of something the league clearly wants to make permanent. Netflix holds the Wednesday-night slot through the 2029 season, and the streamer is treating the debut like a tentpole: pregame coverage begins at 6 p.m. ET, and U2 headlines the halftime show, celebrating the band's 50th anniversary. It's the kind of halftime booking usually reserved for the Super Bowl, dropped into a Wednesday night in November.

The full Thanksgiving week slate

Tonight is just the opener. Five games stretch from Wednesday through Friday, each on a different platform:

Wed, Nov. 25: Packers at Rams; 8 p.m.; Netflix

Thu, Nov. 26: Bears at Lions; 1 p.m.; CBS / Paramount+

Thu, Nov. 26: Eagles at Cowboys; 4:30 p.m.; FOX

Thu, Nov. 26: Chiefs at Bills; 8:20 p.m.; NBC / Peacock

Fri, Nov. 27: Broncos at Steelers; 3 p.m.; Prime Video

Thursday's tripleheader opens with Chicago at Detroit at 1 p.m. ET on CBS, the traditional early kickoff, before Philadelphia visits Dallas and Kansas City closes the holiday at Buffalo. The Black Friday game — Denver at Pittsburgh — wraps the week.

NFL · Nov 24, 2026 · 11:45 PM ET

Steelers bench Aaron Rodgers — Mason Rudolph starts Friday, and a 22-year career may have just ended

By Matt

Pittsburgh announced late Tuesday night that Mason Rudolph will start Friday's Black Friday game against the Broncos — and that Aaron Rodgers will be inactive. One day earlier, Mike McCarthy had said Rodgers was his quarterback.

Disclosure: this post contains affiliate links. I earn a commission on qualifying purchases.

The move

The Pittsburgh Steelers benched Aaron Rodgers on Tuesday night.

In a statement posted by the team on X from senior director of communications Burt Lauten, Pittsburgh announced that Mason Rudolph will start Friday's Week 12 game against the Denver Broncos — and that Rodgers will be inactive for the game. USA Today, Fox Sports, Sports Illustrated, theScore, Heavy and Pro Football Rumors all confirmed the announcement within the hour.

"The Pittsburgh Steelers have named Mason Rudolph the starting quarterback for the game this Friday against the Denver Broncos," the statement read. "Aaron Rodgers will be inactive for the game on Friday."

According to The Ringer's Tom Pelissero, the decision was made by head coach Mike McCarthy and was performance-based — a coach's decision, not an injury call.

The reversal

What makes this stunning is how fast it happened.

On Monday, one day before the announcement, McCarthy was asked whether he had considered turning to Rudolph with the offense struggling. "Aaron Rodgers is our quarterback," he replied, per ESPN's Brooke Pryor. There had been no prior public indication that Pittsburgh was considering a change at quarterback in the middle of a playoff push.

By Tuesday night, the change was made anyway.

The numbers behind it

Rodgers has started 10 games for Pittsburgh this season, completing 60.9% of his passes for 2,241 yards, 16 touchdowns and six interceptions, with an 86.6 passer rating.

The slide came after the Week 9 bye. The Steelers have dropped back-to-back games to the Cincinnati Bengals and the Philadelphia Eagles, and the offense has stalled badly enough that the calls for a change were getting loud before the team made one.

Sunday's 19-16 upset loss to the Eagles was the breaking point. Rodgers completed 30 of 44 passes for 227 yards and a touchdown with no interceptions — a clean line on paper — but the throws barely traveled. His 0.5 air yards per attempt in the first half was the lowest recorded in 20 years, per FOX Sports' Ralph Vacchiano, and FOX's Henry McKenna wrote that Rodgers "is terrified of throwing downfield."

He has also been sacked 31 times through 10 games, and over the last two weeks Rodgers ranks 26th in success rate among quarterbacks.

The replacement

Rudolph is no stranger to this building. Pittsburgh drafted him in the third round in 2018, and he has spent most of his career with the Steelers, appearing in 38 games with 19 career starts. His last start came in 2025 against the Chicago Bears, in relief of an injured Rodgers.

He now gets the start in a game with significant postseason ramifications for both teams: the Steelers host the Broncos on Black Friday, with Pittsburgh sitting at 6-4 and chasing a playoff spot.

What it means

Rodgers announced before the season that he would retire at the end of the 2026 campaign, and he re-signed with Pittsburgh in May after leading the Steelers to a division title in his first year there. He turns 43 in December.

That context is why this benching lands the way it does. Fox Sports framed it plainly: Rodgers "has potentially played the final snap of his legendary 22-year NFL career." Pelissero put it the same way, noting the 42-year-old four-time league MVP "may have played the final snaps of his Hall of Fame career."

Nothing is final yet — the team has said only that Rodgers is inactive for Friday, not that he is done. But a healthy scratch for a quarterback who declared this his final season, benched by the same coach who re-signed him and publicly backed him 24 hours earlier, is not a one-week experiment. It reads like the end.

Friday will tell us whether it is. Rudolph starts. Rodgers watches. And a career that began in 2005 may have ended on a Tuesday night in November, announced in two sentences on social media.

Call of Duty just extended its launch-month sales streak to 19 straight years — and it did it in a down market

By Matt

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 was the best-selling game in the US in October, extending the franchise's run of topping the chart in its launch month to a 19th consecutive year — a streak that began with World at War in 2008.

Disclosure: this post contains affiliate links. I earn a commission on qualifying purchases.

Some streaks survive because the competition is weak. This one survived the opposite. Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 was the best-selling game in the United States in October 2026, according to Circana's monthly sales report — extending the franchise's run of topping the US chart in its launch month to a 19th consecutive year.

The number comes from Circana senior director Mat Piscatella, who publishes the monthly US market report. GameSpot reported the result on Tuesday, and Nintendo Life, VGChartz and GamesIndustry.biz all carried the same Circana figures. It is not a projection from a single outlet. It is the industry's standard sales tracker, and it says Call of Duty did it again.

The streak, and where it started

The run began in November 2008, when Call of Duty: World at War outsold Guitar Hero: World Tour and Gears of War 2 to become the best-selling game of its month. Every Call of Duty release since — across four console generations, three publishers' eras of the franchise, and a calendar that moved launch month from November to October this year — has topped the US chart in the month it launched. Modern Warfare 4, released October 23 on PS5, Xbox Series X|S, PC and Nintendo Switch 2, is the latest.

October's top three tells the rest of the month's story. Gears of War: E-Day finished second and Star Wars: Galactic Racer third, with EA Sports FC 27 fourth — and six of the month's ten best sellers were new releases. Call of Duty beat a crowded field, not an empty one.

A win in a shrinking month

What makes this one different from the other 18 is the market it landed in. Total US spending on video games fell 12% year over year in October, to $4.2 billion. Content sales were down 14%, mobile down 16%, and console content down 18%, per Circana — the comparison dragged down by last October, when Battlefield 6 and Pokémon Legends: Z-A launched in the same window. Hardware was the one bright spot, up 2% to $357 million, with the Switch 2 still leading the market in both units and dollars.

So the streak did not survive on a rising tide. It survived a month where almost everything else shrank. That is the kind of detail that separates a habit from a record.

The catch, and what's next

There is one wrinkle worth stating plainly. Despite winning October, Modern Warfare 4 did not crack Circana's year-to-date top 10 for 2026 — the first time that has happened to a Modern Warfare title since the original's era. October was a strong month, but a single month does not make a year.

And the November chart will not belong to Call of Duty. GameSpot's own read on the month ahead is blunt: GTA 6, which launched November 19, is all but certain to take November and finish 2026 as the year's best-selling game overall. The streak is about launch months, not calendar years — and November was never Call of Duty's month to win this time.

But the record stands on its own terms. Nineteen years, nineteen launch months, nineteen times at No. 1. No other franchise in the Circana era has done anything like it.

Martha Firestone Ford dies at 101 — the matriarch who held the Lions for six decades

By Matt

The Detroit Lions announced Tuesday night that owner and chair emeritus Martha Firestone Ford has died at 101 — two days before the 8-2 Lions host the Bears on Thanksgiving at Ford Field, the stadium she helped rebuild.

Disclosure: this post contains affiliate links. I earn a commission on qualifying purchases.

The news

The Detroit Lions announced Tuesday night that Martha Firestone Ford, the team's owner and chair emeritus, has died at her home in Grosse Pointe, Michigan, surrounded by her family. She was 101.

The team posted the announcement to its official website on Tuesday evening. The Associated Press, USA Today, NBC Sports and Fox News all confirmed the death within the hour. No cause of death was given.

She died two days before the Lions host the Chicago Bears on Thanksgiving at Ford Field — a game that will decide first place in the NFC North, with both teams at 8-2. She was still attending games this season, including a win over the Minnesota Vikings earlier this month.

The steward

Ford's connection to the Lions spanned more than six decades. In 1963, she and her husband, William Clay Ford, purchased full control of the franchise. When he died in 2014, she assumed sole control of the team, and in 2020 she transitioned to emeritus status, with her daughter Sheila Ford Hamp taking over as principal owner and chair.

Her six seasons as principal owner were the steadiest stretch the franchise had known in years. The Lions reached the playoffs twice under her watch, in 2014 and 2016, and in 2017 she made a significant investment in Ford Field that the team credits as the foundation of the gameday environment Lions fans enjoy today.

The family succession is already in place. Her four children — Sheila Ford Hamp, Martha Ford Morse, William Clay Ford Jr. and Elizabeth Ford Kontulis — all hold ownership roles with the franchise, and the team said Tuesday that the family "proudly carries forward the legacy established by Mr. and Mrs. Ford."

The life

She was born Martha Parke Firestone in Akron, Ohio, on September 16, 1925 — the granddaughter of Harvey S. Firestone, founder of the Firestone Tire and Rubber Company. She graduated from Vassar College in 1946 and married William Clay Ford the following year. The couple moved to the Detroit area in 1949 and became fixtures of the city for the next 77 years.

Her work outside football was quiet and constant. She expanded Detroit Lions Charities, served as a longtime trustee of Henry Ford Health, held leadership roles with the Merrill Palmer Skillman Institute, University Liggett School, the Children's Home of Detroit and the Edsel and Eleanor Ford House, and founded the Henry Ford Maplegrove Center. In January 2019 she helped launch Detroit Lions Inspire Change, the team's social justice initiative in the city.

In March 2019, as part of the NFL's 100th-season celebration, she starred in the NFL Films documentary A Lifetime of Sundays alongside the league's other matriarchs — Virginia Halas McCaskey of the Bears, Patricia Rooney of the Steelers and Norma Hunt of the Chiefs.

What it means

Ford never got to see the Lions reach a Super Bowl — the one milestone that eluded the franchise across her entire tenure, through the lean years and into the current revival. She did live to see the turnaround: the team she handed to her daughter is 8-2, contending for the NFC's top seed, and playing its biggest Thanksgiving game in years on Thursday.

She is survived by her four children, 14 grandchildren and 17 great-grandchildren.

Reds bring Tyler Stephenson home — three years, $30 million, and the catching hole is closed

By Matt

Cincinnati re-signed its longest-tenured player on Tuesday night, keeping catcher Tyler Stephenson on a three-year deal with an opt-out after year two — the fifth free-agent catcher this decade to command a three-year guarantee.

Disclosure: this post contains affiliate links. I earn a commission on qualifying purchases.

The move

The Reds finally made their move — and they made it with the player who has been there longer than anyone else on the roster.

Cincinnati and catcher Tyler Stephenson agreed to a three-year, $30 million contract on Tuesday night, ESPN's Jeff Passan first reported, with the deal including an opt-out after the second season and pending a physical. The Cincinnati Enquirer confirmed the agreement through sources, and MLB Trade Rumors, theScore, NBC Sports and Sports Illustrated all corroborated the terms within the hour.

For a team that had looked for nearly a month like it planned to sit out the pre-lockout free agency period entirely, this is a significant strike — exactly one week before the current collective bargaining agreement expires on December 1 and a widely anticipated owners' lockout shuts down baseball business indefinitely.

The player

Stephenson is the longest-tenured player on the Reds' roster, and the only uniform he has ever worn is theirs. Cincinnati drafted him 11th overall in 2015, he debuted in the pandemic-shortened 2020 season, and he has now played 688 big-league games — every one of them as a Red.

The 30-year-old is coming off the best season of his seven-year career by wins above replacement, slashing .241/.323/.404 with 15 home runs, 22 doubles and 54 RBI across 130 games. For his career he is a .257/.335/.422 hitter in just under 2,500 plate appearances.

He is not a perfect catcher — the defense grades out below average and staying healthy has been a recurring battle into his thirties — but the bat plays at a position where offense is scarce, and the Reds know exactly what they are getting.

The summer that made this make sense

This deal only makes sense in the context of July.

Stephenson looked like a trade candidate at the deadline, and he was visibly emotional in a postgame interview when asked about the possibility of being dealt out of the only organization he has ever known. The Reds held him anyway. At the time, the speculation was that they kept him because they believed they could bring him back in free agency — and because they had not held contract extension talks with him in a year and a half, the reunion was anything but certain.

Tuesday night closed that loop. The team that refused to trade him is the team paying him to stay.

The market

Cincinnati did not have much choice but to pay up. The catching market was thin before free agency opened and thinner within days: Ryan Jeffers, considered the top free-agent catcher at the outset, accepted a qualifying offer from Minnesota, leaving Stephenson and the Cubs' Carson Kelly as the top two available backstops.

That scarcity is priced into the deal. Stephenson becomes just the fifth free-agent catcher this decade to command a three-year guarantee — and the only one of that group to also get an opt-out clause. The Reds will roll with a Stephenson–Jose Trevino pairing behind the plate for a third straight season, with top prospect Alfredo Duno — the organization's No. 1 prospect — expected to take over as the everyday catcher in the next few seasons. Stephenson's presence buys Duno time and gives him a veteran to learn from.

What it means

The Reds were one of the least active teams since free agency opened — they could not even keep veteran closer Emilio Pagan, who opted out of the final $10 million year of his deal and quickly signed a one-year, $11.5 million contract with Detroit — and they had just lost reliever Sam Moll to the Cubs hours before the Stephenson news broke.

This is their first big move of the offseason, and it solves their most glaring hole. A team that would have had a gigantic hole at catcher if Stephenson signed elsewhere now has its starter locked up through 2029, with an escape hatch after two years if either side wants one.

For Stephenson, the deal keeps him in the only organization he has ever known — the one that drafted him as a teenager, the one he nearly got traded away from in July, and the one that just made him its catcher of the present while its catcher of the future finishes developing.

Jannik Sinner underwent knee surgery Tuesday — and the Australian Open comeback he was targeting is now in doubt

By Matt

Jannik Sinner confirmed Tuesday he had minor surgery on his right knee after months of rehab failed — a procedure that likely rules him out of the Australian Open in January, the tournament he had circled for his comeback.

Disclosure: this post contains affiliate links. I earn a commission on qualifying purchases.

The surgery

Jannik Sinner confirmed Tuesday that he has undergone surgery on his right knee, extending an absence from tennis that has already lasted more than four months.

"Over the past few months, together with my team we've tried everything to treat my injury without surgery," Sinner wrote in a statement shared on social media. "After some very encouraging progress early on, my knee unfortunately didn't respond as we'd all hoped, that's why today I underwent a minor surgery to improve the condition of my iliotibial band."

The procedure was performed in Turku, Finland, by orthopaedic surgeon Lasse Lempainen, and involved lengthening the iliotibial band — the strip of connective tissue that runs along the outside of the thigh to the knee.

Sinner is the world No. 2 and a five-time Grand Slam champion. He has not played a competitive match since July 12, when he beat Alexander Zverev to retain his Wimbledon title.

The timeline

The recovery is estimated at around three months, according to The Athletic, with one knee specialist telling Sky Sport it could stretch to four. Either way, the math is brutal: the Australian Open main draw begins on January 17, and Sinner is a two-time champion in Melbourne.

That makes him unlikely to feature at the first Grand Slam of 2027 — and rules him out of the February hard-court events as well, with a return to full training pencilled in before Indian Wells in March, where he is the defending champion.

The turn is sharp because the comeback had a date. As recently as November 10, speaking in Milan, Sinner said he hoped to be back in Melbourne, and to play a few tournaments beforehand. Two weeks later, he was on an operating table instead.

The months that led here

This was not a sudden decision. Sinner has been managing inflammation of the iliotibial band for months, trying conservative rehabilitation first. As late as October, a spokesperson for him said he had not undergone surgery and was not planning to do so at that time.

The knee has barely let him move, by his own recent admission. "The worst part for me about this injury is that I cannot compete, I cannot play tennis," he said.

The layoff has already cost him plenty. During his absence he lost the world No. 1 ranking to Zverev, the man he beat in the Wimbledon final. He also had his tonsils removed during the time away and has been rebuilding muscle after losing a significant amount of weight.

"I really miss being on court and will now begin my recovery process together with my team," Sinner wrote. "Thank you for all your support. See you soon!"

What it means

Melbourne was supposed to be the comeback story — the two-time champion returning to the tournament where he has been at his best, after half a year away. Now the first Grand Slam of 2027 will almost certainly go on without him, and the question shifts from when he returns to how much of the early season the knee costs him.

The encouraging part is the word Sinner himself used: minor. This was a procedure to fix a band that months of treatment could not, not a reconstruction. If the recovery holds to the estimate, Indian Wells in March is the realistic target — a full eight months after his last match.

For now, the wait that began at Wimbledon in July stretches into the new year.

ARC Raiders' Flickering Flames event is live — Celeste's dinner, three stages, and the Nessuno Set

By Matt

Store Update 2.7.0 is live in ARC Raiders, and Part 1 of the Flickering Flames project is underway — Celeste is gathering all four contradas in Speranza for a celebration of light, and Raiders have three stages to complete to get her dinner ready.

Disclosure: this post contains affiliate links. I earn a commission on qualifying purchases.

Flickering Flames is live. Embark Studios rolled out Store Update 2.7.0 for ARC Raiders on November 24, 2026, and Part 1 of the two-part Flickering Flames Raider project is underway in Speranza — no restart required, the update is already live in-game.

The premise is the warmest the game has ever been. For the first time, Celeste is bringing members of all four contradas together for a celebration of light, and she is preparing a special dinner to mark it. Raiders help her get it ready across three stages, and each stage pays out weapons and weapon mods. The project runs through December 28, and Part 2 unlocks on December 8.

The three stages

Stage 1 — Banquet Basics. Hand over 10 Durable Cloth, 10 Batteries, 5 Pop Triggers, and 5 Candleberries. Completing it awards a Grappling Hook, a Harmonica, an Il Toro IV shotgun, and a Shotgun Choke II.

Stage 2 — Lights and Tableware. The shopping list gets rarer: 5 Advanced Electrical Components, 2 Silver Teaspoon Sets, Firefly Burners, and 10 Candleberries. The payout is an Anvil IV, an Extended Barrel II, a Tether Launcher, and a Mountaineer's Detector.

Stage 3 — Clear The Way. No scavenging for the final step — instead, pick one of two objectives. Heal three Raiders outside your own squad, or deal 800 damage to fire-wielding ARC — the Vaporizer, Firefly, and Fireball machines. Finishing it, and with it Part 1 of the project, awards a Canto IV, a Compensator III, an Angled Grip III, and a Padded Stock.

Candleberries are the thread running through the whole project, and they grow on bushes during the Cold Snap map condition — which is back in rotation for the event, covering the Rust Belt in snow. If you are short on berries, a Cold Snap run is where to look.

The Nessuno Set hits the store

The Nessuno Set arrives in the in-game store rotation with the update: an outfit, a backpack, and a backpack charm. It is the store side of 2.7.0 — the project itself is the free, playable half, and the cosmetics are the part you buy.

A holiday event, not a patch

There is no balance pass or bug-fix list attached to 2.7.0. It is a store update and a seasonal event, a week after Live Update 2.6.0 did the heavier lifting — bringing Cold Snap back, expanding buried-item hunting to nearly every map, adding the Outlaw Weapon Stencil Set, and putting the game at 50% off for Black Friday. That sale is still running on most platforms through the end of the month and into early December.

The timing is the point. A year after launch, ARC Raiders is running a holiday event built around a dinner, not a boss fight — a communal moment in the settlement while the surface stays hostile. Part 2 arrives in two weeks, and the cosmetic half of the event lands with it.

NHL · Nov 24, 2026 · 9:09 PM ET

Lindholm scores four as Bruins beat Capitals 7-5

By Matt

Elias Lindholm scored four goals — the first four-goal game of his NHL career — as the Bruins outlasted the Capitals 7-5 in a wild Saturday night at TD Garden, snapping Boston's three-game home skid.

Disclosure: this post contains affiliate links. I earn a commission on qualifying purchases.

Elias Lindholm had never scored four goals in an NHL game before Saturday night. He fixed that in about two hours, and the Boston Bruins needed every one of them — beating the Washington Capitals 7-5 in a wild, back-and-forth game at TD Garden that snapped Boston's three-game home losing streak.

Lindholm finished with five points on six shots, adding an assist to the four goals, and three of the goals came the same way: deflections in front of the net, the kind of dirty-area work that rarely makes a highlight reel but wins games.

How the night unfolded

Washington struck first. Tom Wilson opened the scoring at 8:03 of the first period, and Boston answered on the power play when David Pastrnak fired a shot from the point and Lindholm tipped it past Charlie Lindgren at 12:42 — four seconds into the man advantage — to tie it 1-1. Alex Tuch's short-handed goal at 15:58 sent the Capitals into the intermission up 2-1.

The second period was chaos: six goals, four of them Boston's. Pastrnak tied it at 2:01, Tanner Jeannot tipped home the go-ahead goal at 6:23, and Lindholm made it 4-2 at 8:54, racing onto a long Morgan Geekie feed — with an assist for goaltender Jeremy Swayman, his first point of the season — and roofing the puck past Lindgren. Washington answered back to 4-4 on goals from Pierre-Luc Dubois and Dylan Strome, but Lindholm completed his hat trick at 18:24, deflecting a Connor Clifton point shot glove-side to send Boston into the third up 5-4.

Elias Lindholm: 4; 1; 5; 6 shots, +3, 19:42

David Pastrnak: 1; 2; 3; Assisted on two of the four

Morgan Geekie: 0; 3; 3; Three assists

Charlie McAvoy: 0; 3; 3; 300th career assist on the night

The fourth came early in the third. At 4:07, Pastrnak set Lindholm up for another tip-in — his second deflection of a Pastrnak shot on the night — and this time the hats finally rained down properly. Jakob Chychrun cut it to 6-5 on a late power play, but Fraser Minten's empty-netter at 18:34 sealed it.

A first in his career

The night was a first on two counts. It was Lindholm's first four-goal game, and the hat trick that came with it was his third in the NHL — but his first since October 2021, so long ago that the TD Garden crowd barely reacted to it. Only one hat hit the ice after the third goal; fans weren't sure it counted until the fourth went in and the hats poured down.

He's now the fourth Bruin since 2000 to score four in a game, joining Patrice Bergeron, Pastrnak, and Marat Khusnutdinov — and the third to do it since 2021. The outburst also capped a hot month: Lindholm has 10 points in eight games in November.

Lindholm laughed about the missing hats afterward. "It was all good," he said. "One was enough. It was all good."

The top line carried it

Lindholm didn't do it alone. The top line of Geekie, Lindholm, and Pastrnak combined for 11 points, with Pastrnak and McAvoy each posting three of their own. Ten different Bruins got on the scoresheet, and Swayman made 30 saves for his 11th win of the season.

The win moved Boston to 15-7-1 and ended a skid that had started to feel like a slide. Washington, which came in having lost four straight, fell to 10-11-0 — and left TD Garden having been beaten, in the end, by a guy standing in front of its net.

Apex Legends veterans' studio Gravity Well is shutting down — without ever releasing a game

By Matt

Gravity Well, the anti-crunch studio founded by Apex Legends veterans Drew McCoy and Jon Shiring, is going into 'hibernation' after losing its funding in the spring — six years in, its debut game never saw the light of day.

Disclosure: this post contains affiliate links. I earn a commission on qualifying purchases.

Gravity Well is done. The studio founded in 2020 by former Apex Legends executive producer Drew McCoy and lead software engineer Jon Shiring updated its website on November 24 to say it is going into "hibernation" — the polite word for a studio that has run out of money and out of road. Six years after it opened its doors, Gravity Well is closing without ever releasing a game.

The statement, signed by McCoy, Shiring, and chief operating officer Mon Saetern, is blunt about what happened. "In the Spring of 2026 we lost our funding support, and like so many other studios this year, we were unable to secure replacement funds to keep the team on to finish our game." The studio added that it still believes in the project it was building, and called the team it assembled "truly world class" — then turned the statement into a job reference, telling hiring managers that any Gravity Well resume that lands on their desk "comes with our highest recommendation." Publishers and investors interested in the game are invited to get in touch.

The warning signs were there in October

The hibernation announcement did not come out of nowhere. On October 6, Gravity Well confirmed it had laid off more than 40 people — the majority of its team — after losing its funding over the summer. The studio described the cuts as a "fight for survival" and admitted at the time that "given the current state of the industry our future is uncertain." It kept going with a skeleton crew while it searched for a new backer. That search has now failed.

What the team was actually making remains a mystery. Gravity Well never formally unveiled its debut title, though reporting at the time of the layoffs described it as a brand-new IP believed to be a third-person shooter. The studio released just two pieces of concept art for the game — one of them the coastal town and seaplane image above — and that is effectively all the public ever saw of it.

A studio built on a promise the industry couldn't keep

Gravity Well launched with a pitch that stood out at the time: a remote-native studio where team health was the top priority, crunch was off the table, pay was good, and every developer had real creative freedom. McCoy said at the time that the point was to "shake things up in AAA game dev." The founders brought serious pedigree — both had worked on Call of Duty, Titanfall, and Apex Legends at Respawn — and the studio planned to stay deliberately small, peaking at around 80 people.

It was a bet on a funding climate that no longer exists. The studio was one of many formed during the pandemic-era investment boom, when money flowed freely into new teams. As that money dried up, those studios have been falling one by one — Gravity Well is only the latest, and its story is the bleakest version of the pattern: not a game that flopped, not a studio bought and gutted, but a team that never got to show anyone what it made.

The door is technically still open. "Hibernation" is not "closed," and the statement leaves room for a publisher or investor to revive the project. But with the team scattered and the funding gone, what Gravity Well built now exists only as two pieces of concept art and a recommendation letter.

Tyler1 lasted one week on League's new voice chat before Riot banned him

By Matt

League's team voice chat launched November 18. One week later, Tyler1 — one of the game's biggest streamers — got hit with three punishments at once for what he said on it, live on his own stream.

Disclosure: this post contains affiliate links. I earn a commission on qualifying purchases.

League of Legends finally gave every player a microphone — and it took Tyler1 one week to get banned for what he said into it.

Tyler Steinkamp, better known as Tyler1, picked up three punishments at once: a three-day ban from League itself, a seven-day suspension from voice chat, and a 30-day suspension from the League Partner Program. He found out about it live on his own Twitch stream, mid-game, the same way his audience did.

What happened on stream

The ban traces back to a clip from his stream that went viral. Playing with a randomly matched teammate on Nami, Tyler1 repeatedly insulted the player on the new team voice chat — at one point telling his teammate to kill themselves, then covering it up by verbally drumming over the words.

His defense, delivered on stream after the ban landed: he was joking around with the Nami player, they laughed about it afterwards, and the game was a stomp anyway. "Context doesn't matter apparently," he said, repeatedly, while railing against the severity of the punishment.

Riot's side of it is straightforward. When the company announced team voice chat, it said from the start that voice conversations would be recorded and could lead to in-game punishments. A report option for voice abuse was built into every reporting menu from day one. Tyler1 tested the system in its first week, on camera, in front of millions of followers — and the system did exactly what Riot said it would do.

The feature was seven days old

Team Voice arrived November 18 with Patch 26.23, and it is the biggest change to how League players talk to each other since the game launched. Before this patch, voice chat only worked inside a premade party. Now any player can talk to their whole team — randomly matched strangers included — during champion select and in game, in every queue except Classic.

The rollout is deliberately narrow for now: North America and Oceania only, with other regions to follow once Riot trusts the moderation tooling. It is push-to-talk only, players below Honor level 3 can listen but not speak, and five optional Voicemod voice skins let players change how they sound to their team. Riot framed the whole thing as a test, and said it would expand only as it gained confidence in moderation.

Tyler1 is the test's first famous failure. That is the part that matters for everyone else: the moderation is not theoretical, it is not slow, and it does not care how big your stream is. One week, one viral clip, three punishments.

The same story as 2016 — and the opposite

There is history here, and it is the reason this ban landed the way it did. Tyler1 first became famous for getting banned. In April 2016, Riot handed him an indefinite, identity-level ban — no League account, ever, under any name — after a documented history of verbal abuse and harassment, with a Riot employee calling him a "genuine jerk" in the announcement. He spent 613 days in exile, streaming variety content and running his own Tyler1 Championship Series, before Riot lifted the ban in January 2018. His return stream peaked at more than 382,000 concurrent viewers, a non-tournament record on Twitch at the time.

Since then he has been the redemption story Riot points to: a partner, a regular on official broadcasts — he even appeared on the Worlds 2026 final broadcast this month — and a streamer who built his brand on having cleaned up his act. That is what makes the partner-program suspension the sharpest of the three punishments. A three-day game ban is a weekend off. A 30-day suspension from the League Partner Program is Riot saying, publicly, that the reformed-Tyler1 story has a crack in it.

He is not the only one testing the new lines, either. Fellow streamer TheBausffs was also suspended recently for feeding, which suggests Riot is enforcing the new voice-chat era quickly and visibly rather than letting the first month slide.

The question now is whether the ban changes anything. Tyler1 has been here before — banned, furious, insisting it was a joke — and the last time, the ban made him bigger. This time the stakes are smaller and the message is narrower: the microphone is on, it is being recorded, and the first week proved it.

Broncos suspend J.K. Dobbins one game for conduct detrimental — he won't travel to Pittsburgh

By Matt

Sean Payton announced Tuesday that Denver's veteran running back is suspended for Friday's Black Friday game against the Steelers — one snap on Sunday, then a closed door.

Disclosure: this post contains affiliate links. I earn a commission on qualifying purchases.

The suspension

The Denver Broncos have suspended running back J.K. Dobbins for one game, head coach Sean Payton announced at his Tuesday press conference.

"I'm suspending J.K. Dobbins for this weekend's game," Payton told reporters. "Conduct detrimental. That's all I'm going to say about it. Coach's decision."

He took no follow-up questions. The suspension is Payton's decision, not the league's — a team-imposed ban, and the coach made it clear he is not explaining it further.

Dobbins will miss Friday's Black Friday game against the Pittsburgh Steelers in Week 12, will not practice this week, and will remain away from the team throughout its preparation, according to reports from Denver.

The snap that started it

The ban comes two days after the strangest line of Dobbins' season. In Denver's 38-24 win over the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday, the veteran played a season-low one offensive snap — a single carry, stuffed for no gain.

The backfield belonged to someone else. Rookie Jonah Coleman handled the bulk of the rushing workload, turning 24 carries into 111 yards and three touchdowns in the same game Dobbins barely touched the field.

Payton would not connect the two things publicly, and the specifics of whatever happened between the coach and the running back remain under wraps. But the sequence is hard to ignore: a healthy veteran goes from starter to one snap, and two days later he is suspended.

It is a sharp turn even by the standards of this backfield. On Monday, Payton told reporters Dobbins was healthy and "going to be super important for what we're doing in this stretch." By Tuesday, he was suspended.

The fall from RB1

Dobbins opened the season as Denver's No. 1 running back, and he earned that role. Last season, when healthy, he was the main man in the Broncos' rushing game, running for 772 yards and four scores across 10 games.

This year the ground has steadily shifted under him. Coleman has taken more and more of the work as the weeks have gone on, and with RJ Harvey on injured reserve, the rookie — not the veteran — is now the feature back. Dobbins is 27, and he has bristled before at being framed as an aging player: after a win over the Cardinals in Week 7, he told reporters, "You keep calling me a vet. I'm not old. I'm 27 years old. Not old. I'm not 30. I'm not even close to 30."

Now the 27-year-old will watch Friday's game from home while the rookie who replaced him carries the backfield into Pittsburgh.

What it means

For Friday, the picture is simple: Coleman leads the Broncos' backfield against the Steelers, with Dobbins sidelined by his own coach's decision. Denver's ground game has already been trending his way for weeks; the suspension just makes it official for a night.

The bigger question is what comes back with Dobbins next week. A one-game, team-imposed suspension for conduct detrimental is a coach sending a message, and Payton sent it in the shortest possible terms. Whether Dobbins returns to a role or returns to the margins will be decided by what happens behind closed doors this week — the part Payton refused to discuss.

Counter-Strike 2 is heading for a ninth straight monthly player drop — and the slide is already the longest on record

By Matt

Counter-Strike 2 is on pace for a ninth consecutive monthly decline in average Steam players, with the eight months already in the books marking the longest slide in SteamCharts history — and the year's final Major, which starts today in Singapore, is the obvious circuit-breaker.

Disclosure: this post contains affiliate links. I earn a commission on qualifying purchases.

Counter-Strike 2 is on pace for a ninth straight monthly drop in average players on Steam — and the eight months already in the books are the longest decline streak in SteamCharts' data, which goes back to July 2012.

The 30-day average sat at 767,092 concurrent players as of November 23, according to SteamCharts data reported by Pley.gg. That is the lowest the average has been since January 2024, when it stood at 760,859. The slide started after February, when the monthly average peaked at 1,084,095 — down 317,003 players, or 29.2%, in the nine months since.

The math on November

November is not over yet, but the arithmetic is brutal. The month-to-date average was running at about 757,000 through the morning of November 23. To finish level with October's 797,324 average, the rest of the month would need to average around 910,000 players — a level no full month has reached since June. The final November figure lands on December 1.

Independent trackers tell the same story. Explosion's tracker puts the 30-day average at 771,144 with November so far down 5% on October, and PixelKrypt has the month-to-date average at 754,893, down 5.3%. The numbers differ slightly by methodology, but every tracker agrees on the direction and the level.

This is not a GTA 6 story

It would be easy to blame the biggest launch in gaming history — and GTA 6 certainly pulled players away from everything last week, with Call of Duty's daily active users falling 42% over launch weekend. But Counter-Strike's slide started in March, eight months before GTA 6 unlocked on November 19. Every single month since February has come in lower than the one before it. This is a slow bleed, not a launch-week blip.

And for all the decline, the game is still enormous. The 30-day peak hit 1,326,695 concurrent players, and the game remains one of the busiest on Steam on any given day. The average is drifting down; the ceiling is still there.

The Major starts today

The timing is either perfect or cruel, depending on your view. The PGL Major Singapore 2026 — the sixth Counter-Strike 2 Major and the 25th Counter-Strike Major overall — opens today, November 24, and runs through December 13. Thirty-two teams are in Singapore for a $1,250,000 prize pool, with the playoffs at the Singapore Indoor Stadium from December 10 to 13 and $500,000 going to the winner. It is the first Major ever held in Southeast Asia and the second CS2 Major of the year.

Majors have always been the game's biggest shop window — the last one is the kind of event that pulls lapsed players back for a few weeks. Whether this one can do more than that, and actually bend a nine-month curve, is the question the next three weeks will answer.

One caveat on the numbers: these figures cover Steam only. Players on Perfect World's Chinese client are not included in SteamCharts' data.

Blue Jays land Japanese ace Kaima Taira on five years, $80 million — the pivot after losing Skubal, Rogers and Peralta

By Matt

Toronto lost out on three pitchers in three days, then pivoted to Japan: Kaima Taira is a Blue Jay on a five-year, $80 million deal.

Disclosure: this post contains affiliate links. I earn a commission on qualifying purchases.

The move

Toronto finally landed a pitcher — just not one of the three it chased first.

The Blue Jays agreed to terms with Japanese right-hander Kaima Taira on Tuesday, the New York Post's Jon Heyman first reported, with ESPN's Jeff Passan, Reuters and USA Today all confirming the agreement. The deal runs five years and includes a $5 million signing bonus and an opt-out after the third season, which would put Taira back on the market before he turns 30. Toronto also owes the Seibu Lions a posting fee of about $13.9 million on top of the contract.

It is the Jays' answer to a brutal three days. They offered Tarik Skubal nine years and $420 million and watched him take $450 million from the Mets. They went after Trevor Rogers, who signed with the Cubs. They went after Freddy Peralta, who signed with the Orioles. Taira costs roughly a sixth of what Skubal got, and with the collective bargaining agreement expiring Dec. 1 and a lockout expected to follow, Toronto did not have time to wait for the market to come back around.

The player

Taira is 27, and he arrives with a resume that reads like two different pitchers stapled together — because it is.

He spent most of his career in Japan moving between the rotation and the bullpen. A year ago he was Seibu's closer and saved 31 games. This season, finally left in the rotation for a full year, he went 12-5 with a 1.36 ERA in 23 games, striking out 141 batters in 146 innings — the lowest ERA of any qualified starter in Japan. He is the first pitcher in Nippon Professional Baseball history to save 30 or more games in one year and win 10 as a starter the next.

The career line backs it up: 37-24 with 62 saves and a 1.85 ERA in 325 appearances, with 620 strikeouts against 226 walks in 592 innings. He was the Pacific League Rookie of the Year in 2020 and a four-time NPB All-Star, and in July 2021 he set an NPB record with 39 consecutive scoreless appearances. In April 2025 he closed out a combined no-hitter with Tatsuya Imai against SoftBank.

The stuff is the selling point. He is 5-foot-8, pitches only from the stretch, and works from a low arm angle with a high-effort delivery — but his release point sits about 6.8 feet in front of the rubber, so his fastball gets on hitters faster than the radar gun suggests. It sits 95-96 mph and touches 99, and he throws as many as seven pitches, with the splitter the one hitters chase most. The question scouts keep asking is the one his frame invites: whether a 5-foot-8 starter with that much effort in his delivery can hold up across a full major league season.

The fit

Toronto knows exactly how much pitching it needs. The Jays went into 2026 with eight starters, and the injuries piled up fast — Trey Yesavage, Shane Bieber and Jose Berrios all opened the year on the injured list, and Cody Ponce and Max Scherzer went down soon after. The club finished last in the AL East a year after its run to the World Series.

Taira likely slots into the third spot in the 2027 rotation, behind ace Dylan Cease — who finished second in AL Cy Young voting after striking out 239 batters in the first year of his seven-year, $210 million deal — and alongside Jose Soriano, Yesavage, Ponce and Spencer Arrighetti. He also gives the Jays something they have not had in a while: a pitcher who can start and, if the rotation ever gets healthy, close.

What it means

This is a bet on translation. The Jays paid a fraction of the Skubal price for a pitcher who dominated the best league in Japan in his first full year as a starter, and the opt-out after year three means Taira is betting on himself too — pitch like he did for Seibu, and he is a free agent again at 29. If the ERA holds up in the American League East, Toronto got a front-line starter for a middle-of-the-rotation price. If it doesn't, the Jays are the team that lost three pitchers in three days and settled for the fourth.

Collectibles · Nov 24, 2026 · 3:09 PM ET

Pokémon ETBs cost double MSRP; Magic boxes cost half

By Matt

NerdSnack's Black Friday price guide, updated November 24, puts 40 sealed products against MSRP — and the two biggest games point in opposite directions: Pokémon boxes run double list price while Magic booster boxes sell for about half of it.

Disclosure: this post contains affiliate links. I earn a commission on qualifying purchases.

Black Friday is Friday, November 27, and this year's card market is split in two. NerdSnack's Black Friday guide, updated November 24, lists the price to beat for 40 Pokémon, Magic, Lorcana and One Piece products — and the two biggest games in the hobby point in opposite directions. Magic booster boxes already sell for about half their MSRP, while a Pokémon 30th Celebration Elite Trainer Box costs more than twice its list price.

The rule the guide uses is simple: a real deal beats two numbers, the product's MSRP and its current TCGplayer market price. If a sale price only beats a crossed-out "list price" the seller chose, it isn't a deal.

The split at a glance

MTG Marvel Super Heroes Play Booster box: $209.70; $102.64; 51% under MSRP

MTG Star Trek Play Booster box: $209.70; $110.82; 47% under MSRP

Lorcana Hyperia City booster box: $143.76; $128.45; 11% under MSRP

Pokémon Delta Reign Elite Trainer Box: $49.99; $74.95; 50% over MSRP

Pokémon 30th Celebration Elite Trainer Box: $49.99; $113.99; 2.3× MSRP

One Piece OP-18 booster box: $119.76; $180.88; 51% over MSRP

Pokémon: the premium side

The 30th Celebration set is this year's big Pokémon gift release, and it's the hardest to find at list price. The ladder runs from a roughly $10 Mini Tin — which still sells for $20.88 to $25.16 — up through a $66.27 Booster Bundle and the standard Elite Trainer Box. The Pokémon Center version of that box is the steepest climb of all: $249.93 against a $59.99 MSRP.

Delta Reign, which came out November 6, is the newest set and the most reasonable of the current Pokémon releases. Its standard ETB sits at $74.95, and the guide's advice is to hold out for an MSRP restock rather than pay the marketplace price — the Pokémon Center, Target and Best Buy all sell at MSRP when stock drops. Older main sets have settled closer to list: Pitch Black, Chaos Rising and Perfect Order booster boxes now sit only 6–9% above MSRP, so a Black Friday box under about $165 is a strong price. The outlier is Phantasmal Flames, whose ETB is $138.02 — nearly three times MSRP almost a year after release.

A second guide, Tabletop Meta's Pokémon Black Friday roundup, tells the same story from a different snapshot: on November 18, every recent set's Elite Trainer Box and Booster Bundle sold above MSRP on TCGplayer, with the 30th Celebration box at $110.58.

Magic: the bargain side

Magic is the opposite of Pokémon this year. Most sealed product already sells below MSRP, and even Star Trek — which came out November 13 — trades well under it. The Marvel Super Heroes Play Booster box is the cheapest box in the guide at $102.64, about half its list price, and the Star Trek Play Booster box has kept falling since launch, from $132.48 on October 22 to $110.82.

The one Magic exception is the Star Trek Beam Me Up Bundle, which still sells above its $99.99 MSRP at $152.73. A Star Trek Commander deck, at $32–$73 against a $74.99 MSRP, is a ready-to-play gift for a Commander player.

Lorcana and One Piece

Lorcana's newest set, Hyperia City (out October 16), is a rare case where the booster box sells below MSRP. The gift products go the other way: the Beast Gift Box sells for $66.59 against a $29.99 list price, more than double. The guide's advice is to look for it at big-box stores before paying marketplace prices.

One Piece is the priciest side of the market. Boosters list at $4.99 a pack, so a 24-pack box costs $119.76 at MSRP — but every recent box trades far above that, from OP-18 at $180.88 up to OP-17 at $266.12. A box at or near MSRP usually means a local game store on release day, not a Black Friday sale.

How to tell a real deal from a fake one

Presale prices are the biggest trap in the guide. When it was first published on October 22, a Delta Reign Elite Trainer Box cost $106.29 on presale; today it's $74.95, about 29% less. An OP-18 booster box dropped from $353.77 to $180.88 once it was in stores. The same warning applies to what's coming next: Lorcana's Into the Inkdark booster box already lists at $294.05 on TCGplayer, about double MSRP, more than two months before its February 2027 release.

TCGplayer itself hasn't announced a 2026 sale yet, as of November 24. Last year it ran a four-day "Cyber Weekend" with 10% back in store credit on everything, and subscribers got 13% or more. If the timing holds, the 2026 sale would run from Friday morning, November 27, to Monday night, November 30 — but store credit only saves money on a later TCGplayer order, so it's worth the most if you'll buy again before Christmas.

Three big card releases landed in the past three weeks — Delta Reign on November 6, MTG Star Trek on November 13, and One Piece OP-18 on November 20 — and all three are now past launch day, with prices cooling since presale. That's the window Black Friday sits in: new enough that stock exists, old enough that the launch-day markup has started to fade. The numbers above are the line to beat.

T1 win the OWCS Asia Finals 4-1 — back-to-back titles and the No. 1 seed for the World Finals

By Matt

T1 beat Crazy Raccoon 4-1 in the OWCS Asia Finals grand final in Busan, winning their first Asia title two weeks after their first Korea title — and locking in the No. 1 Asian seed for the World Finals in Guangzhou, December 2–6.

Disclosure: this post contains affiliate links. I earn a commission on qualifying purchases.

T1 are the champions of Asia. The Korean squad beat Crazy Raccoon 4-1 in the grand final of the 2026 Overwatch Champions Series (OWCS) Asia Finals on Sunday, November 22, at the BEXCO Auditorium in Busan — winning their first OWCS Asia title and going back-to-back with the OWCS Korea Stage 3 championship they won two weeks earlier.

The final was played in front of a live crowd at G-STAR 2026, the Korean game show, and T1 controlled it from the start. They took the first two maps, Samoa and Neon Junction, before Crazy Raccoon answered on New Junk City. T1 closed it out on Colosseo and then Shambali Monastery, with Crazy Raccoon scraping only a single map in an otherwise dominant effort.

The road to the final

Six teams played the Asia Finals from November 20 to 22: four from Korea — T1, ZETA DIVISION, Crazy Raccoon, and Team Falcons — plus Japan's VARREL and the Pacific's The Gatos Guapos. T1 opened with a 3-0 win over VARREL, then beat ZETA DIVISION 3-1 in the semifinals on Saturday. Crazy Raccoon swept Team Falcons 3-0 in the other semifinal, setting up a rematch of a Korea Stage 3 playoff series the two teams had already fought to the wire.

Kim "DONGHAK" Min-sung and Kim "ZEST" Hyun-woo were singled out as T1's standouts in the final. There were no asterisks this time, either: T1's Korea Stage 3 win had come with question marks over the absence of the hero Doctrine due to a bug. In Busan, T1 simply proved they are in their zone in this meta, with Reaper and Echo dominating the DPS slots and Junker Queen anchoring the tank role across the tournament.

What it means for Guangzhou

The Asia Finals also settled Asia's four seeds for the OWCS World Finals, which run December 2 to 6 in Guangzhou, China. T1, who had already qualified by winning Korea Stage 3, take the No. 1 seed. Crazy Raccoon enter as the No. 2 seed. ZETA DIVISION beat Team Falcons 4-2 in the third-place match to take the No. 3 seed, and VARREL — who edged The Gatos Guapos 3-2 in a fifth-place decider — take the last ticket as the No. 4 seed.

The winner took $25,000 from the $40,000 prize pool. All 12 World Finals teams are now confirmed: T1, Crazy Raccoon, and ZETA DIVISION from Korea; Twisted Minds, Team Peps, and 1234 from EMEA; Dallas Fuel, Team Liquid, and Spacestation Gaming from North America; Weibo Gaming and All Gamers from China; and VARREL from Japan. Twisted Minds arrive as defending champions, chasing back-to-back world titles after winning the 2025 World Finals in Stockholm.

T1 head coach Hee-won "Rush" Yoon kept the focus forward. "The players gained confidence from winning Korea Stage 3, and I am glad we maintained that momentum to win the Asia Finals," he said. "We will showcase great performance at the World Finals as well and bring home the championship."

Two titles in two weeks, a No. 1 seed, and a coach already talking about bringing the championship home. T1 go to Guangzhou as Asia's team to beat.

Orioles land Freddy Peralta on five years, $125 million — the Trevor Rogers replacement, and then some

By Matt

Baltimore lost Trevor Rogers to the Cubs and answered in hours: ALCS MVP Freddy Peralta is an Oriole on a five-year, $125 million deal with no deferrals and no opt-outs.

Disclosure: this post contains affiliate links. I earn a commission on qualifying purchases.

The move

Baltimore did not waste a day mourning its rotation.

Hours after Trevor Rogers left for the Cubs, the Orioles signed right-hander Freddy Peralta to a five-year, $125 million deal, Ken Rosenthal of The Athletic first reported Tuesday morning. Fox Sports confirmed the agreement, and NBC Sports' Rotoworld added the term sheet's cleanest detail: the contract includes no deferrals and no opt-outs over its five years.

It is a direct answer to a direct loss. Rogers, the left-hander who anchored Baltimore's staff, agreed to a five-year, $120 million deal with Chicago on Monday night. The Orioles replaced him before the next morning's coffee got cold — and paid $5 million more to do it.

The player

Peralta is a two-time All-Star, and his 2026 season tells the story of a pitcher who found himself again at exactly the right time.

He started the year with the Mets, where he posted a 4.99 ERA and a 1.48 WHIP over 22 starts. Then Tampa Bay traded for him, and everything changed: a 3.25 ERA and a 1.01 WHIP over 10 regular-season starts for a Rays team that went on to win the American League pennant. In the postseason he was better still, posting a 2.95 ERA across 21 1/3 innings — and winning ALCS MVP honors.

Before all that, he spent eight seasons with the Milwaukee Brewers, from 2019 through 2025, building the resume that made him one of this winter's most wanted arms.

The fit

The Orioles needed this in the worst way. Their rotation finished 27th in baseball in opponent batting average, 26th in WHIP and 17th in ERA last season — a staff that asked its lineup to win shootouts most nights.

Peralta slots straight into the top of that rotation, and he brings something Baltimore's staff has lacked: a pitcher who just proved, on the biggest stage of the season, that his best baseball is happening right now. The Rays version of Peralta — the one with the 1.01 WHIP and the ALCS MVP trophy — is the one the Orioles are paying for.

What it means

The winter's pitching market is moving fast, and the lockout clock is ticking — the collective bargaining agreement expires Dec. 1, and teams are racing to get deals done before signings freeze. Baltimore lost its ace on Monday and replaced him on Tuesday, at full price, with no games attached to the money.

That is not a team rebuilding. That is a team that watched the Rays ride Peralta to a pennant and decided it wanted the next ride to be its own.

Guardians bet $17.5 million on Kris Bubic — a one-year splash for a franchise that rarely makes them

By Matt

Cleveland agreed to a one-year, $17.5 million deal with 2025 All-Star Kris Bubic on Tuesday, betting the left-hander's shoulder is behind him and his 3.02 ERA is real.

Disclosure: this post contains affiliate links. I earn a commission on qualifying purchases.

The move

Cleveland does not do this often — which is exactly why this one stands out.

The Guardians agreed to a one-year, $17.5 million contract with left-handed pitcher Kris Bubic on Tuesday, Ben Nicholson-Smith of Sportsnet first reported, with ESPN's Jeff Passan confirming the agreement and MLB's Mark Feinsand among the reporters corroborating it. Passan's summary said it plainly: the 2025 All-Star heads to one of the best pitching organizations in baseball on a big one-year number.

For a franchise that almost never splashes in free agency, $17.5 million for one season of a pitcher is a statement. The short term softens the risk. The number says they believe in the arm.

The player

Bubic's case is a bet on the pitcher he was before his shoulder gave out.

He pitched just 55 innings in 2026 after missing a big chunk of the season with a shoulder injury, and he was traded from Kansas City to the Dodgers at the deadline. When he finally got back on a mound in September, he fired 4 2/3 scoreless innings for Los Angeles — a small sample, but a clean one.

Go back a little further and the upside is obvious. Since the beginning of last year, Bubic has a 3.02 ERA with 167 strikeouts against 65 walks in 166 2/3 innings over 29 starts. That is a mid-rotation starter's line, and the All-Star nod in 2025 says the league noticed.

The fit

Cleveland still needs to solidify its rotation for 2027, and Bubic projects to slot in as a No. 3 or No. 4 starter — a real arm in the middle of the staff, not a lottery ticket at the back of it.

That is also the Guardians' whole model: take a pitcher with good stuff and a good track record, put him in one of baseball's best pitching-development organizations, and let the infrastructure do the rest. If the shoulder holds, $17.5 million for one year of a 3.02 ERA starter is a bargain. If it doesn't, the deal is over in twelve months.

What it means

The Guardians are not usually the team writing checks like this in November. That they did — a day after their first signing of the offseason — says they see a window and they are not waiting for the lockout to close it.

Bubic gets a one-year stage in the best possible place to rebuild his value. Cleveland gets a proven starter at a price that only stings if he can't stay on the mound.

Cubs land Japanese Triple Crown winner Teruaki Sato on six years, $120 million — $240 million in 12 hours

By Matt

Hours after landing Trevor Rogers, the Cubs struck again: Japanese slugger Teruaki Sato is headed to Chicago on the second nine-figure deal of a wild 12 hours.

Disclosure: this post contains affiliate links. I earn a commission on qualifying purchases.

The move

The Cubs are spending like a team that believes its window is now.

Hours after landing Trevor Rogers on Monday night, Chicago agreed to terms with Japanese slugger Teruaki Sato on Tuesday morning, ESPN's Jeff Passan first reported. The deal is for six years, with Fox Sports, the New York Post, theScore and MLB Trade Rumors all confirming the agreement. MLB Trade Rumors put the scale of the spree plainly: the Cubs have now committed $240 million in the span of about 12 hours.

Sato was posted by the Hanshin Tigers on Nov. 1, which opened a 45-day window for major league teams to negotiate with his representatives. Chicago won the race before that window closed — and before the collective bargaining agreement expires on Dec. 1, with a lockout expected to follow.

The player

Sato is 27 — he turns 28 at the start of the 2027 season — and he arrives with the kind of resume that does not need translating.

He is a two-time Central League MVP who won the 2025 NPB MVP Award, and this year he won the Triple Crown for Hanshin, hitting .306 with 39 home runs and 106 RBIs across 143 games. Over the last two seasons he has averaged 39.5 home runs, 104 RBIs and a .594 slugging percentage per year. He played six seasons for the Tigers, from 2021 through 2026, and suited up for Japan in the 2026 World Baseball Classic.

He was primarily a third baseman in Japan, but that is not where Chicago plans to play him. Passan reports Sato is expected to play a corner outfield spot for the Cubs, and the New York Post lists him as a corner outfielder and designated hitter.

The fit

The outfield needed the help. Seiya Suzuki and Ian Happ are both free agents, and the Cubs' corner spots were the softest part of a roster that won 89 games last season, made the playoffs for a second straight year, and was swept by the San Diego Padres in the National League Wild Card Series.

Sato gives them a middle-of-the-order bat who has already produced at an elite level against professional pitching — just in a different league. The Cubs will also owe a posting fee to Hanshin on top of the contract, which does not count against the competitive balance tax threshold.

What it means

Two signings, two nine-figure commitments, one night. The Rogers deal fixed the rotation. This one fixes the lineup. Together they say the Cubs are not waiting for the lockout to end to get better — they are doing it now, while the market is moving.

The risk is the one every Japanese star carries on arrival: the numbers are real, but they were put up in NPB, and the adjustment to major league pitching is the question no scouting report can fully answer. The Cubs just bet nine figures that the Triple Crown translates.

Scott Pilgrim is officially coming to Fortnite — the creator confirmed it himself

By Matt

Scott Pilgrim is coming to Fortnite, and the confirmation came from the top: series creator Bryan Lee O'Malley revealed the crossover himself in an 18-image Instagram post that ends on the Fortnite battle bus. No date or pricing yet — but the files are already in the game.

Disclosure: this post contains affiliate links. I earn a commission on qualifying purchases.

Scott Pilgrim is coming to Fortnite. The confirmation did not come from a leaker or a datamine — it came from series creator Bryan Lee O'Malley himself, who revealed the crossover in an 18-image post on his Instagram account on November 23.

The post is a slow zoom-out. The first image shows Ramona Flowers holding Scott Pilgrim's hand as the two fall from the sky. Each slide pulls back a little further on the strange object in the distance until the outline resolves into something unmistakable: the Fortnite battle bus, the vehicle that drops players onto the island at the start of every match. O'Malley did not add a date or any details. He did not need to. The bus is the announcement.

What the files say — and what they don't

Dataminers dug into the latest Fortnite update and found the cosmetics the collaboration is expected to bring: two skins, one emote, two pickaxes, and two instruments — a bass and a drum kit. The skins are expected to be Scott and Ramona, which fits the teaser. The instruments are where it gets interesting, and where the leaks stop being a straight line. Scott plays bass in his band Sex Bob-Omb, so the bass is his. Ramona does not play an instrument. Kim Pine is the drummer. So either the drums belong to Kim — meaning the crossover includes more characters than the teaser shows — or the instrument set is just a bundle and the logic does not matter. Either way, the cosmetics themselves are still unconfirmed by Epic, and so is everything about how they will be sold.

An earlier leak pointed the same direction. On November 12, veteran leaker HYPEX flagged an encrypted file found during downtime for update 43.10, with cosmetics matching Scott and Ramona — two skins with LEGO variants, back blings, and an emote built around the Power of Love sword. At the time Epic had said nothing. Now the creator has said it himself, which moves the whole thing from "leaked" to "confirmed, details pending."

Why this one lands differently

Fortnite's recent crossovers have leaned hard into anime, and Treasure Hunters is the peak of that: the One Piece crew has been rolling out in waves since the season launched November 1. Scott Pilgrim is a lane change. The franchise started as O'Malley's graphic novel series, became the 2010 cult film Scott Pilgrim vs. the World, and expanded again into the Netflix animated series Scott Pilgrim Takes Off, produced by Science Saru. It is a story about a bass player in a Toronto band fighting his crush's seven evil exes — funny, scrappy, and twenty years into its cult status. It fits Fortnite's anything-goes island, but it is not another anime tie-in. It is a comic-book world dropping into a battle royale.

Epic has not announced an official release date, V-Bucks pricing, or bundle contents for the Scott Pilgrim crossover. The teaser is official, the files are in the game, and the creator has confirmed it — so the launch should not be far off. When it lands, the question will not be whether Scott and Ramona show up. It will be whether Kim Pine and the rest of the band come with them.
